body:
Why do we measure health?

The human body continuously regulates blood circulation, energy supply, body temperature, nutrition and the delivery of oxygen to tissues. These processes allow organs and cells to function normally. Changes in body functions may sometimes be detected through measurable signs before a person develops noticeable symptoms.

Health measurements provide information about particular body functions or health risks. Blood pressure, body mass index, blood glucose and haemoglobin are common measurements used in health assessment. The glycaemic index is related to nutrition, but it describes the effect of carbohydrate-containing food rather than measuring a person's body.

What does each measurement tell us?

MeasurementWhat it representsUsual unit
Blood pressure (BP)Pressure exerted by circulating blood against arterial wallsmm Hg
Body mass index (BMI)Body weight relative to heightkg/m2
Blood glucoseConcentration of glucose in bloodmg/dL
Glycaemic index (GI)Relative blood-glucose-raising effect of a carbohydrate-containing foodIndex value
Haemoglobin (Hb)Concentration of the oxygen-carrying protein in bloodg/dL

How are these measurements connected to body functions?

Blood circulation and oxygen transport

The heart pumps blood through the circulatory system. Blood flowing through arteries exerts pressure on their walls. This pressure changes as the heart contracts and relaxes, producing the 2 values reported in a blood pressure reading.

Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, a protein that binds oxygen in the lungs and helps carry it to body tissues. Blood pressure and haemoglobin therefore describe different aspects of circulation. Blood pressure concerns the force of blood against arterial walls, while haemoglobin concerns the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.

Nutrition and energy supply

Carbohydrates in food are digested into simpler sugars, including glucose. Glucose is absorbed into the bloodstream and used by cells as an important energy source. The body regulates blood glucose through hormones, especially insulin and glucagon.

Blood glucose measurements indicate how much glucose is present in blood at a particular time. The glycaemic index, in contrast, helps describe how rapidly a carbohydrate-containing food raises blood glucose compared with a reference food.

Body weight and height

Body mass index relates a person's weight to height. It is useful for identifying broad weight categories and possible health risks. Unlike a blood glucose or haemoglobin test, BMI does not measure the concentration of a substance in blood.

Understanding units correctly

mm Hg means millimetres of mercury. It is a unit of pressure and is commonly used for blood pressure.

mg/dL means milligrams per decilitre. It expresses the amount of a substance, such as glucose, in a given volume of blood. A decilitre equals 100 mL.

g/dL means grams per decilitre. Haemoglobin is commonly reported in this unit.

kg/m2 means kilograms per square metre and is used for BMI. The glycaemic index is a relative numerical index and does not have a physical unit such as mg/dL.

A measurement is not always a diagnosis

A screening measurement may indicate increased risk, but its interpretation depends on factors such as age, sex, pregnancy, symptoms and the circumstances of measurement. A single unusual reading does not always establish a disease.

Why normal measurements do not guarantee complete health

A person can have normal blood pressure but low haemoglobin. Another person can have a BMI within the international healthy-weight category but elevated blood glucose. Each measurement examines a different characteristic.

For example, a resting blood pressure of 118/76 mm Hg and a fasting glucose level of 95 mg/dL both fall within commonly used adult reference categories. However, neither result establishes that the person's haemoglobin concentration or overall nutritional status is normal.

Prelims focus

  • BP measures arterial pressure and is expressed in mm Hg.
  • BMI relates body weight to the square of height.
  • Blood glucose is commonly reported in mg/dL.
  • Haemoglobin carries oxygen and is commonly measured in g/dL.
  • GI describes a carbohydrate-containing food, not a patient's blood glucose concentration.
  • Trap: Blood pressure, pulse rate and haemoglobin concentration are different measurements.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 11, Transportation in Animals and Plants, pp. 121–125, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 13, Why Do We Fall Ill?, pp. 176–178, 2018–19 edition; US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Adult BMI Categories, 19 March 2024, consulted 3 November 2026; Diabetes UK, Glycaemic Index and Diabetes, last reviewed 22 September 2025, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Understanding Everyday Health Measurements

body:
What is blood pressure?

Blood pressure (BP) is the pressure exerted by circulating blood against the walls of arteries. The heart generates this pressure by pumping blood into the arterial system.

Arteries have elastic walls that expand when blood is pumped into them and help maintain blood flow between heartbeats. Blood pressure therefore changes during each cardiac cycle.

Systolic and diastolic pressure

A blood pressure reading contains 2 numbers, such as 120/80 mm Hg.

  • Systolic blood pressure (SBP): The upper number. It represents arterial pressure when the ventricles contract and pump blood into the arteries.
  • Diastolic blood pressure (DBP): The lower number. It represents arterial pressure when the ventricles relax between contractions.

The contraction phase of the heart is called systole, while the relaxation phase is called diastole.

Thus, a reading of 120/80 mm Hg means a systolic pressure of 120 mm Hg and a diastolic pressure of 80 mm Hg. These are pressure values, not counts of heartbeats.

What is normal blood pressure?

A reading around 120/80 mm Hg is commonly used as a familiar reference for adult blood pressure. However, precise categories depend on the clinical guideline being used.

The American Heart Association's 2025 adult classification uses the following categories:

CategorySystolic pressureDiastolic pressure
NormalBelow 120 mm HgBelow 80 mm Hg
Elevated120–129 mm HgBelow 80 mm Hg
Stage 1 hypertension130–139 mm Hg80–89 mm Hg
Stage 2 hypertension140 mm Hg or higher90 mm Hg or higher

For normal and elevated categories, the stated systolic and diastolic conditions must both apply. For hypertension categories, either the systolic or the diastolic value can place the reading in that category. When the 2 values fall into different categories, the higher category applies.

For example, 145/76 mm Hg falls into the American Heart Association's Stage 2 category because its systolic pressure is at least 140 mm Hg, even though its diastolic pressure is below 80 mm Hg.

Hypertension and the WHO threshold

Hypertension means persistently elevated blood pressure.

The World Health Organization uses a threshold of systolic pressure at least 140 mm Hg and/or diastolic pressure at least 90 mm Hg for diagnosing hypertension when the elevated readings are confirmed on 2 different days.

Therefore, 140/90 mm Hg is an important WHO recognition threshold. A person need not have both values elevated: persistently high systolic pressure alone or persistently high diastolic pressure alone may satisfy the definition.

The WHO threshold and the American Heart Association's Stage 1 category are not identical. The American Heart Association identifies Stage 1 hypertension beginning at 130 mm Hg systolic or 80 mm Hg diastolic, whereas the WHO diagnostic threshold described above begins at 140 mm Hg systolic or 90 mm Hg diastolic. Questions that name a particular guideline should be answered using that guideline.

Low blood pressure

Hypotension means abnormally low blood pressure. A reading around 90/60 mm Hg or below is commonly described as low blood pressure.

Some healthy individuals naturally have relatively low blood pressure without symptoms. In others, low pressure may cause dizziness, fainting or weakness. Its significance depends on the person's usual blood pressure, symptoms and medical circumstances.

Why blood pressure can change

Blood pressure is affected by several factors, including the force with which the heart pumps, resistance within blood vessels, physical activity, emotional stress and certain medicines.

Exercise and stress can temporarily raise blood pressure. Repeatedly high resting blood pressure is more concerning because sustained pressure can damage blood vessels and increase the risk of heart disease, stroke and kidney disease.

Understanding a reliable reading

Blood pressure can be measured using a sphygmomanometer or a validated electronic blood pressure monitor. Correct conditions help distinguish a person's usual resting pressure from a temporarily altered reading.

  • A person should rest quietly for about 5 minutes before a routine resting measurement.
  • The arm should be supported at approximately heart level.
  • An appropriately sized cuff should be placed on the bare upper arm.
  • Measurements should be repeated when necessary rather than relying on one unusual result.

Blood pressure and pulse rate must not be confused. Pulse rate is the number of arterial pulsations per minute, whereas blood pressure measures force per unit area within arteries.

Indian public-health connection

The India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI) was launched in November 2017 to strengthen the detection, treatment and control of hypertension. It involves the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, state governments, the Indian Council of Medical Research, the World Health Organization and technical partners.

The initiative reflects the importance of identifying persistently elevated blood pressure and providing continuing care through the public-health system.

Prelims focus

  • Systolic pressure is measured during ventricular contraction.
  • Diastolic pressure is measured during ventricular relaxation.
  • A familiar adult reference reading is approximately 120/80 mm Hg.
  • WHO hypertension recognition threshold: at least 140 mm Hg systolic and/or 90 mm Hg diastolic, confirmed on different days.
  • The American Heart Association's 2025 Stage 1 category begins at 130 mm Hg systolic or 80 mm Hg diastolic.
  • Trap: Elevated systolic pressure can identify hypertension even when diastolic pressure is not elevated.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 11, Transportation in Animals and Plants, pp. 121–125, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Biology, Class 11, Body Fluids and Circulation, section on cardiac activity, GPSC Biology compendium Volume 34, pp. 105–113; WHO India, Hypertension, definition and India Hypertension Control Initiative sections, consulted 3 November 2026; American Heart Association, 2025 High Blood Pressure Guideline, Top Things to Know, item 4, consulted 3 November 2026; American Heart Association, Home Blood Pressure Monitoring, consulted 3 November 2026; MedlinePlus, Low Blood Pressure, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Blood Pressure: Meaning, Normal Values and Hypertension

body:
What is body mass index?

Body mass index (BMI) is a numerical measure that relates body weight to height. It is commonly used to classify adults into broad weight categories and to identify possible weight-related health risks.

A person's weight alone does not indicate whether that weight is relatively high or low for their height. BMI provides a simple way to consider both measurements together.

How is BMI calculated?

BMI = weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres.

Its unit is kg/m2.

For example, consider an adult weighing 60 kg with a height of 1.60 m.

Square of height = 1.60 × 1.60 = 2.56 m2.

BMI = 60 ÷ 2.56 = 23.4 kg/m2, approximately.

The calculation uses height in metres, not centimetres. A height of 160 cm must first be expressed as 1.60 m.

International adult BMI categories

The following internationally used adult categories are presented by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and are consistent with conventional WHO BMI classifications.

BMI categoryBMI in kg/m2General interpretation
UnderweightBelow 18.5Relatively low weight for height
Healthy weight18.5 to below 25.0Conventional healthy-weight category
Overweight25.0 to below 30.0Elevated weight-related health risk
Obesity30.0 or higherGreater likelihood of weight-related health problems

In a typical multiple-choice question using international adult categories, BMI 17.5 indicates underweight, BMI 22 indicates healthy weight, BMI 27 indicates overweight and BMI 32 indicates obesity.

Why height matters

Two people with the same body weight can have different BMI values if their heights differ. Because height is squared in the calculation, a taller person generally has a lower BMI than a shorter person of the same weight.

Consider 2 adults who each weigh 64 kg. At a height of 1.60 m, BMI is 25.0 kg/m2. At a height of 1.80 m, BMI is approximately 19.8 kg/m2.

According to the international adult classification, the first value is at the lower boundary of the overweight category, while the second falls in the healthy-weight category.

BMI and health risks

High BMI is associated with an increased likelihood of several conditions, including type 2 diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular disease. However, BMI is a screening measure and does not directly measure body fat percentage, blood pressure or blood glucose.

For example, a muscular athlete may have an elevated BMI because muscle contributes substantially to body weight. Conversely, a person with a BMI in the conventional healthy range may still have excessive abdominal fat or other metabolic risk factors.

BMI should therefore be interpreted alongside other health information rather than treated as a complete assessment of health.

Special relevance for Indian and other Asian populations

Research has found that some Asian populations experience increased risks of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease at BMI values below the conventional international overweight threshold of 25 kg/m2.

A WHO expert consultation published in 2004 retained the international BMI categories but identified additional public-health action points at 23.0 and 27.5 kg/m2, among others, for considering health risks in Asian populations.

These action points are not identical to the standard international overweight and obesity categories. A question asking for the conventional WHO international overweight threshold should be answered with BMI 25.0 kg/m2. A question specifically referring to Asian population risk assessment may use lower action points.

There is no single BMI value that perfectly separates healthy and unhealthy individuals. Risk varies among populations and individuals, and different guidelines may use different assessment thresholds.

When standard adult BMI categories should not be used

Children and adolescents are still growing. Their BMI is interpreted using age- and sex-specific reference standards rather than applying the usual adult categories directly.

Pregnancy also changes body weight for reasons that are not adequately represented by ordinary adult BMI classification.

Prelims focus

  • BMI is calculated as weight in kg divided by height in metres squared.
  • International adult underweight category: BMI below 18.5.
  • International adult healthy-weight category: BMI 18.5 to below 25.0.
  • International adult overweight category: BMI 25.0 to below 30.0.
  • International adult obesity category: BMI 30.0 or higher.
  • Trap: BMI does not directly measure body fat, and Asian population risk action points are not the same as the international category boundaries.

[Sources: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Adult BMI Categories, 19 March 2024, consulted 3 November 2026; WHO Expert Consultation, Appropriate Body-Mass Index for Asian Populations and Its Implications for Policy and Intervention Strategies, The Lancet, Volume 363, Issue 9403, pp. 157–163, 10 January 2004; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 10, Reaching the Age of Adolescence, section on growth and height, pp. 113–116, 2018–19 edition.]
